newsitem.title: POLAND: FOCUS - POLISH FLOOD CALLS FOR TIGHTENING - C.BANKER.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - POLISH FLOOD CALLS FOR TIGHTENING - C.BANKER.

text.p: Polish central bank chief Hanna Gronkiewicz-Waltz said on Thursday heavy flooding which savaged the country's south and west called for an even tighter monetary policy than earlier planned.
"Even before the flood, actions were needed to limit money supply and the disaster makes such actions even more necessary," Gronkiewicz-Waltz told Reuters in an interview.
"This disaster may force us to make our policy even more restrictive because we cannot allow that on the top of the flooding we also have a flood of money," she added.

On Thursday the parliament authorised the government to borrow an extra 2.5 billion zlotys from the central bank to finance relief operations and remove the damage of 11-day flooding which has claimed 46 lives and inundated 4,500 sq kms.

She said the National Bank of Poland (NBP) would keep pushing market interest rates higher and consequently jack up its official rates to contain booming credit and offset monetary effects of its emergency credit line for the government.
"Real interest rates will keep on growing and we should forget for many months about rate cuts while there is a very real possibility of a rise in official rates," she said.
"Credit growth is still high and market rates are so close to the lombard rate that everything indicates that we will have to raise nominal rates," she added.
The central bank has kept its official lombard and discount rates unchanged at 25 and 22 percent respectively for a year.
Gronkiewicz-Waltz said a recent flight of foreign investors from the region in the wake of the late-May Czech crown crisis allowed more flexibility in interest rate adjustments.
She said that at least until the September 21 parliamentary polls there was little risk that higher rates would attract speculative capital from abroad.
But she said relatively thin investor portfolios made the bank less concerned about the future of the zloty, which took a dive this week.
"Because investors have left the region following the Czech crisis there is no substantial risk for the zloty," she said.

The zloty tumbled five percent on Tuesday as concerns over the impact of the flooding coincided with growing investor uneasiness over Poland's widening trade gap, upcoming elections and a general reluctance to invest in the region.
After partial recovery on Wednesday it again showed signs of nervousness on Thursday, closing at 3.4900 to the dollar or about four percent below the trading band centre.
Gronkiewicz-Waltz said another nervous market reaction was possible if a forecast second wave of flooding hit Poland.
But she stressed the bank was not greatly concerned with large zloty swings as long as it stayed within its 14-percent trading band and saw little risk of having to widen the band.

Gronkiewicz-Waltz said it was too early to predict the impact of a weaker zloty on Poland's trade deficit and on inflation but said inflationary pressure could be offset by slower crawling devaluation of the zloty.
The zloty is now being devalued by one percent per month against a basket of five Western currencies.
But she stressed the NBP would wait with considering such a move until the situation stabilises. "Today is not the right moment for such decisions," Gronkiewicz-Waltz said.

She said it was too early to estimate the economic impact of the floods but said they would certainly slow economic growth from the expected six percent this year and possibly result in higher inflation than the 12-13 percent earlier predicted for December.
